learn.title: What makes a good hash
learn.body: A good hash function is fast, gives the same result for the same key, and spreads keys evenly over the table. If many keys land in the same slots, the table slows down. Keys that are strings must first be turned into numbers.

learn.title: Add up the letters
learn.body: A first try: add the character codes. Easy, but anagrams add up to the same number.

learn.title: Mix with a multiplier
learn.body: Multiplying by 31 before adding makes position matter. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around, which is fine here.

learn.title: Hashing cat by hand
learn.body: The multiplier version, before the final `% 8`.
steps: h after c is 99. After a, 99 x 31 + 97 = 3166
98262 % 8 is 6, so cat goes in slot 6

learn.body: Never use the memory address of a string as its hash. Two equal strings at different addresses would hash differently.

questions.prompt: Which is a property of a good hash function?
choices: It returns a different number each call
questions.explanation: Even spread keeps slots lightly filled.

questions.prompt: Why is adding up letters a weak hash for words?
questions.explanation: Order is ignored, so cat, act and tac all add up to 312.

questions.prompt: The sum hash adds character codes. cat adds up to 312. What is 312 % 8?
questions.explanation: 312 is 39 times 8, so the remainder is 0.

questions.prompt: What does multiplying by 31 each step add?
choices: Position in the word affects the result
questions.explanation: The same letters in different order produce different totals.

questions.prompt: The same key must always give the same hash, so the function must be \_\_.
questions.explanation: Determinism lets you find again what you stored.

questions.prompt: In the multiplier version, cat hashes to 6 with table size 8. What is the table size's job?
choices: It limits the index to 0 through 7
questions.explanation: The final % 8 reduces any large number into a valid slot.
